summary: Marps is a route planner for Mars. Pick any place on the planet, on a flat map or a globe, and Marps opens a 50 × 50 km map of it built from NASA Mars Trek data. Click a start and an end point, and it finds the route that takes the least effort for an astronaut on foot or a crewed rover. It avoids steep slopes and hard ground such as boulder fields and loose dune sand, which it scores from three orbital datasets: a geologic map, night-time infrared and dune fields. Like a map app on Earth, it compares that route with the shortest one, estimates walking and driving times, gives turn-by-turn rover directions, and lets you slide along the route to see the elevation, slope and ground at every point. On Mars, the shortest way is not always the safest: Spirit's mission ended after the rover became stuck in soft soil. Marps makes that judgement quick, visual and free, as a Windows app that needs no installation.
details:
What it does and how it works

  1. Choose a place. Type a latitude and longitude, or double-click anywhere on the flat map or the globe.
  2. Map the area. Marps downloads the 50 × 50 km area from NASA Mars Trek: elevation from the MOLA–HRSC blended model (200 m), as a grid of 251 × 251 points. Mars Trek reprojects the data around the area's own center, so every cell is a true 200 m square, even near the poles.
  3. Score the ground. Each of the 250 × 250 squares gets a "ground ease" score from 0 (hardest) to 1 (easiest). Three datasets go into it:
    • the USGS geologic map of Mars (SIM 3292), which gives each type of terrain a base score;
    • THEMIS night-time infrared, which shows how firm the surface is: rock stays warm at night, while dust and sand cool quickly;
    • the Mars Global Digital Dune Database, which caps loose sand at a very low score.
  4. Find the route. The grid becomes a network of points, each linked to its 16 nearest neighbors. Dijkstra's algorithm finds the path with the lowest cost: distance along the ground plus a penalty for climbing and descending. The penalty is heavier on hard ground. Slopes steeper than the ground allows are ruled out: 10° on the hardest ground, up to 30° on the easiest. The result is a smooth curve along the route.
  5. Compare. A second route, the shortest one, ignores slopes and ground, then is checked against the same limits. A table compares the two: time, distance, climb, steepest slope, ground ease, and how much of each route is too steep.
  6. Time it.
    • Walking uses Tobler's hiking function, scaled for a pressurized suit (about 3 km/h on flat, easy ground).
    • The rover does 10 km/h on the flat, slowing on slopes up to 25°.
    • Hard ground slows both. Walks longer than an 8-hour spacewalk are flagged.
  7. Explore. A slider, an elevation chart with a ground-ease strip, and a rover you can drag or play along the route show the conditions at every point. Rover directions warn about dunes, steep slopes and rough ground. Heatmaps show elevation and ground ease, and 1,772 IAU place names and 74 landmarks, including nine missions' landing sites, help you find your way.

Downloads run in the background and are saved on the computer, so areas open in a second or two and routes appear in under a second.

Benefits

  • Shows trade-offs instantly. In one test in Gale crater, the shortest route was 0.8 km shorter but climbed more than twice as much (295 m against 137 m) and took 12 minutes longer by rover.
  • Points out hazards: dune sand, steep slopes and rough ground.
  • Helps plan time, including whether a walk fits in one spacewalk.
  • Needs no specialist knowledge or software. It runs on an ordinary Windows laptop and is free and open source (GPL-3.0).

Intended impact

Marps gives mission planners, scientists, students and the public a quick first look at how to cross a piece of Mars, and why a route matters. It shows how NASA's open datasets can be combined to judge how easy ground is to cross. It is a tool for early planning and learning, not a replacement for detailed engineering studies with higher-resolution images.

Tools and technology

  • Python: PyQt6 and Qt WebEngine (desktop app), NumPy, SciPy (graph search), Pillow.
  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS: Leaflet 1.9 for the map, and our own canvas renderer for the globe.
  • NASA Mars Trek web services: elevation, geology, dunes, infrared, imagery and place names, all downloaded while the app runs.
  • PyInstaller to package the Windows app. VS Code with Live Share for teamwork. Git and GitHub.
  • No special hardware: developed and tested on Windows laptops.
  • We used Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant, through Claude Code) to help write, test and package the code. Our AI_DISCLOSURE.md file records what it did in every file.

What makes it creative

  • It brings the conventions of a familiar map app to another planet: alternative routes, walking or driving, turn-by-turn directions and travel times.
  • It uses night-time infrared as a measure of how firm the ground is, and combines it with geology and dune maps into one score for how easy ground is to cross.
  • The steepest allowed slope depends on the ground underfoot.
  • Each area is drawn in its own map projection, so distances and areas are true anywhere on Mars, including the poles.
  • The globe is physically based. The planet darkens towards its edge, has a thin dusty atmosphere, and sits against a star field that follows the statistics of the real night sky.

Factors we considered

  • Safety: slope limits, loose sand, rough ground and spacewalk length.
  • Data: NASA Mars Trek data downloaded while the app runs and saved for next time.
  • Honesty: the scores and times are estimates from orbital data, and the README states the limits. For example, the infrared data covers 65° S to 65° N.
  • Ease of use: familiar controls, loading indicators, and a single zip with no installation.
  • Reliability: background loading, saved downloads, and clear messages when Mars Trek can't be reached.
  • Openness: a free license, credits for all data and libraries, and a full record of how AI was used.
